stances.claim: The rule of law is besieged on three parallel fronts: the Philippine legal system (alleged inability or unwillingness to investigate crimes against humanity), the US courts (almost 100 horrendous cases against Trump), and the ICJ (ground-war genocide cases from Ukraine v. Russia and South Africa v. Israel).

The ICJ (UN organ since 1945, 193 member states, state-vs-state cases) is distinct from the ICC (Rome Statute, 2002, 123 member states, individual crimes against humanity) -- though both are based in The Hague -- and the US and China are members of ICJ but not ICC, with significant consequences for what each can adjudicate.

The Ukraine-Russia ICJ case demonstrates the rule-of-law dilemma starkly: ICJ rulings are 'legally binding but could not be enforced by the Court' -- Russia ignored the March 2022 interim order to stop offensive -- and yet the order 'emboldened' the EU, UK, Australia, US, and allies to send arms, medicine, and food to Ukraine. Russia's invocation of the rule of law in accusing Ukraine of genocide is itself a perverse use of the same standard.

The South Africa-Israel ICJ case (Jan. 26, 2024, 15-2) issued six commands equivalent to a 'preliminary mandatory injunction' directing Israel to prevent harm to Palestinian civilians, ensure military compliance, punish incitement, deliver basic services, prevent destruction of war-crime evidence, and submit a report within 30 days -- and Israel's response will be 'a great challenge to the faith of the free world in the rule of law.'

The Trump cases pose three rule-of-law questions: (1) how Scotus will decide the Colorado disqualification appeal (Trump's lawyer 'incredibly argued' Jan. 6 was 'a riot, not an insurrection'); (2) how Scotus will decide the appeal from the CA rejection of presidential immunity (the CA held immunity adheres only to INCUMBENT chief executives); (3) whether the courts will decide before November or procrastinate, since 'if they would just wait and Trump wins, all the cases may be dropped due to the presidential immunity of an INCUMBENT president.'

If the Scotus disqualifies Trump and he refuses to obey -- instead leading 'a more destructive insurrection or a full-scale rebellion' -- the test will be whether Republicans and Trumpsters 'respect the rule of law and obey faithfully, though grudgingly, their highest court.'

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban frames the rule of law as 'besieged' on three parallel fronts: the Philippine legal system (alleged inability or unwillingness to investigate crimes against humanity), US courts (almost 100 horrendous cases against Donald Trump -- 'the most SUIT-able presidential aspirant in US history,' per his Jan. 15 column), and the International Court of Justice (ICJ) overwhelmed with ground-war cases. He first untangles the ICJ from the ICC: both are based in The Hague, but the ICJ (UN organ since Oct. 24, 1945, with 193 member states) tackles state-vs-state litigation, while the ICC (Rome Statute, in force July 1, 2002, with 123 member states) tackles crimes against humanity brought against individuals -- and the US and China are members of the ICJ but not the ICC. The Ukraine-Russia case shows the rule-of-law paradox starkly: Russia accused Ukraine of genocide in Donetsk and Luhansk to justify its February 2022 invasion; the ICJ issued an interim order in March 2022 directing Moscow to stop, which Russia ignored -- yet the order 'emboldened the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, the US, and their allies to send military arms, medicine, and food to assist Ukraine,' even as Russia perversely invoked the rule of law to justify its invasion. On Jan. 26, 2024, the ICJ ruled 15-2 that it has jurisdiction over South Africa's accusation that Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza; while declining to order a ceasefire, it issued six commands equivalent to a 'preliminary mandatory injunction': prevent killing/harming Palestinian civilians, ensure military compliance, punish incitement, deliver basic services, prevent destruction of war-crime evidence, and submit a report within 30 days (by Feb. 26). 'Will Israel follow the rule of law and submit its report?' CJ awaits 'with bated breath the Jewish response' -- 'a great challenge to the faith of the free world in the rule of law.' On the Trump cases, the Scotus is taking up the Colorado disqualification appeal (Trump's lawyer 'incredibly argued' on Feb. 8 that the Jan. 6 Capitol assault was 'a riot, not an insurrection'); separately, the Scotus will decide an appeal from a US Court of Appeals ruling rejecting Trump's defense of presidential immunity (the CA held immunity 'adheres only to an INCUMBENT chief executive') -- but the bigger question is whether the courts will decide before November or simply procrastinate, because if they wait and Trump wins, 'all the cases may be dropped due to the presidential immunity of an INCUMBENT president.' If the Scotus disqualifies Trump and he refuses, leading 'a more destructive insurrection or a full-scale rebellion,' the test will be whether Republicans and Trumpsters 'respect the rule of law and obey faithfully, though grudgingly, their highest court.' (Forward-pointer: 'The rule of law in the South and North China Sea in a future column.')
